section: 1. A prettier plot is not a smallest-n argument
text:
1. A prettier plot is not a smallest-n argument
I asked:

They looked better. But I didn’t know it we need the smallest defensible n. Maybe then going off visually isn’t right?

AI said (response summary): Visual evidence is useful, but a nicer larger-n plot does not explain why a smaller candidate is unacceptable. Compare nearby values using plots, diagnostics and theory, and acknowledge borderline choices rather than inventing a sharp cutoff.
What changed: AI added population-specific smaller-n boundary experiments for both seeds, retaining B = 10,000. The reports compare below/at/above values and explain reservations. For example, die 9 versus 10 is explicitly borderline, not a proved failure at 9.
How it was checked: AI ran the saved-vector validation against each seed’s CSV. The refined evidence stays in the eight investigations and the PDF’s boundary section. I questioned the reasoning; I did not personally discover the underlying code defects or independently audit every integer.

section: My role and the important distinctions
text:
My role and the important distinctions
I specified the research question, populations, R/Quarto requirement, seed and no-invented-results rule. I questioned whether better-looking plots justified the smallest n, requested clearer answers, and required a readable final report. AI generated the code, proposed working boundaries, found technical defects and ran the checks.
Our review clarified that n counts observations in one sample and B counts fresh Monte Carlo samples, not bootstrap resamples. A correct mean/SE does not establish a Normal shape. Cauchy’s population mean and variance are undefined, although a finite sample average can be calculated. Independent Normal observations have an exactly Normal average at every positive n. These are the important concepts explained during review; this log does not claim complete line-by-line mastery or independent confirmation of every boundary.

Validation record

Full reproduction: October 6, 2026
A fresh temporary checkout excluded the local R library, sample-mean vectors, figures and rendered reports. AI restored the locked packages with renv::restore() using the package cache, then reran the full workflow with B = 10,000 and seeds 7616/7617. Primary diagnostics, alternate diagnostics, Normal calibration summary and final summary matched the working repository byte-for-byte on R 4.6.1. There are 215 tested population/n rows per seed.
This was same-machine reproducibility, not an independent scientific review or a guarantee of identical bytes on every R/platform version. Later report-only revisions did not repeat this full run or dependency restore.


Technical corrections and checks







What needed attention
Correction / evidence




Alternate runs could overwrite primary plotted vectors
Separate seed directories; both seeds’ saved vectors match CSV B, mean, SD and Q-Q RMSE.


Shared refinement grids and weak smaller-n arguments
Population-specific searches; below/at/above evidence for both seeds; borderline reservations retained.


Discrete histogram bins could mislead
Bins aligned to the sample-mean lattice; Q-Q steps distinguished from curvature.


Cauchy has no valid population moments
No theoretical mean/SE; all-vector Q-Q diagnostics and explicitly labeled central-window histogram.


Machine observations must stay dependent
Exact seeded replay checks the recurrence; no iid SE is assigned. Finite individual moments do not prove a dependent CLT.


Basketball probabilities vary
Endpoint/mean checks and the exact sum of individual Bernoulli variances; n=1 uses p=.90.


Synthetic ages must follow the supplied model
Normalized instructor weights and exact age moments checked; not historical mortality data.


Final table must use actual evidence
Selected and neighboring rows validated; missing/duplicate evidence fails rather than being filled in.


Normal calibration is context
Thirty independent Monte Carlo experiments per coarse n; empirical noise ranges are not pass/fail thresholds.


Reproduction environment
renv setup repaired; dependency versions locked; Quarto supplies Typst.





Report-validation history

October 7: all seven instructor sources were re-read; the expanded PDF and eleven website pages rendered. Every expanded PDF page was inspected, and all 215 primary diagnostic rows were checked at their displayed precision. Instructor files matched their supplied copies.
October 10: the 35-page version was compressed to 14 pages, then reorganized into 13. Model/saved-vector tests passed; rendered metrics, navigation, tables and plots were checked. Both PDF copies matched. Statistical result CSVs and boundaries were not changed by these presentation revisions.
Final cleanup: validation history is consolidated here rather than kept in a separate Markdown file. The final checks below document this revision; historical checks above are not presented as newly repeated full simulations.



Final submission check: October 10, 2026

AI reran the existing R smoke/model and saved-vector tests. Additional checks recomputed skewness, excess kurtosis and theoretical references for all 430 saved diagnostic rows, verified the eight decision summaries, and recomputed the Normal calibration summary. All agreed with the saved outputs; no new simulations were run.
The clarified PDF rendered at 13 pages. AI visually inspected every page and checked the cover index, selected-n/card metrics, boundary comparisons, all eight moment rows, six Exponential seed rows and calibration ranges against the CSVs. Text and figure bounds passed; both downloadable PDF copies matched byte-for-byte.
All 11 HTML reports rendered. Their local links/resources and selected-n diagnostic values passed checks. The README’s eight decisions match the generated summary, and its direct-download link returned a successful response from public GitHub.
Only the README and this log remain as source Markdown documentation. Useful validation history was preserved here before removing the separate file; the redundant rendered README was removed and excluded from regeneration. Obsolete links and the empty template are gone. The R code, results, selected boundaries, instructor references, figures and dependency lockfile were unchanged.

These are AI-run computational and presentation checks, not an independent human audit. The October 6 fresh-directory run remains the full-reproduction record.


Limits
The n choices are explicit practical judgments, not automatically discovered mathematical thresholds. Borderline neighbors remain uncertain; the dependent-process choice does not establish an asymptotic CLT. No unrecorded pre-run prediction, personal surprise, independent audit or complete mastery is fabricated. All three designated extra-credit cases are included, but awarded points remain the instructor’s decision.
The reviewed PDF uses Quarto 1.10.18, bundled Typst and Helvetica Neue on macOS. Font substitution or a different platform can change layout; a page-count change requires review.

4 Special evidence


Code
plot(nonidentical_probabilities(100L), type = "l", xlab = "Shot", ylab = "Probability")









Each n gets a new evenly spaced probability vector; it is not a prefix of one fixed 100-shot sequence. For n >= 2 the mean probability is 0.70, but pretending every shot has p = 0.70 gives the wrong variance.


Code
n <- selected_row(id)$selected_n
p <- nonidentical_probabilities(n)
knitr::kable(data.frame(n = n,
  expected_mean = mean(p),
  correct_SE = sqrt(sum(p*(1-p))/n^2),
  iid_shortcut_SE = sqrt(mean(p)*(1-mean(p))/n)), digits = 4)





n

The difference is mathematical: average[p_i(1-p_i)] equals p-bar(1-p-bar) minus average[(p_i-p-bar)^2]. Therefore the iid shortcut overstates the variance here.

title: Cauchy
text:
iid standard Cauchy; population mean and variance do not exist. The average remains standard Cauchy for every n.
One theoretical check uses the characteristic function: phi(t) = exp(-abs(t)). Independence gives phi(t/n)^n = exp(-abs(t)), the same characteristic function for the average. Thus no finite n produces convergence to Normal.

Decision status: No finite n by theory
Selected N: No finite n: standard Cauchy averages remain Cauchy by theory.
I chose this n because: No finite selection: iid standard Cauchy averages remain standard Cauchy.
Why I did not choose smaller tested values: Increasing n cannot repair the missing finite mean and variance; the ordinary CLT does not apply.
Issue / limitation: Not merely slow: no Normal convergence. Tested through n=5000.
This is a theoretical failure, not an uncertain boundary judgment. Empirical skewness, kurtosis and SD in the table are finite-vector descriptions with no population-moment targets. Standardizing by an outlier-dominated empirical SD can compress the central Q-Q points; it does not rescue Normality.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
I investigated five required populations and all three extra-credit processes, with B = 10,000 separate samples at each n. Normal means are exact at n = 1. The die and synthetic mixture smooth quickly; skew, discrete gaps and dependence require more observations. Cauchy never converges to Normal in this experiment’s iid setting.
My standard is a useful central-shape approximation, not exact Normality or extreme-tail accuracy. I combine histograms, Q-Q plots, numerical diagnostics, valid theory and nearby larger values. Borderline neighbors mean there is uncertainty about the exact smallest integer.
Download the 13-page final report
The report opens with an index, three direct answers on page 2, and actual AI iteration on page 3. It is self-contained for the eight decisions, histogram/Q-Q cards, boundary reservations, appropriate moment checks and seed sensitivity. All three extra-credit investigations are identified at the beginning and on their result cards. These pages retain the detailed progression and important-code explanations.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
I investigated five required populations and all three extra-credit processes, with B = 10,000 separate samples at each n. Normal means are exact at n = 1. The die and synthetic mixture smooth quickly; skew, discrete gaps and dependence require more observations. Cauchy never converges to Normal in this experiment’s iid setting.
My standard is a useful central-shape approximation, not exact Normality or extreme-tail accuracy. I combine histograms, Q-Q plots, numerical diagnostics, valid theory and nearby larger values. Borderline neighbors mean there is uncertainty about the exact smallest integer.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
4 What I take from this
The surprising contrast is that a complicated synthetic population can smooth faster than a simple skewed distribution. Discrete steps are not automatically a failure. Matching a mean and SE does not establish a Normal shape. Dependence changes variance reasoning; non-identical independent shots need individual variances. Heavy tails can invalidate the ordinary CLT altogether.
Each separate investigation includes population shape or process behavior, retrospective theory expectation, important code explanations, boundary plots and both-seed diagnostics. The expectation is not presented as a personal prediction made before the original simulations.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
5 Reproducibility and AI
The seed is 7616, with fixed sensitivity seed 7617. Methodology, AI exchanges and validation, the repository README and original instructor references document the workflow. Judgment inputs live in results/decisions.csv; scripts/finalize_summary.R validates boundary evidence and copies generated diagnostics into the summary. It does not infer normality from a single test or metric.

title: Methodology
text:
For a candidate sample size n, one repetition generates n observations and computes one sample mean. Repeating this B = 10,000 times produces the simulated sampling distribution of the sample mean.
The project uses a coarse-to-fine search. The initial grid is deliberately broad; earlier exploratory centers are retained for reproducibility. Targeted population-specific grids in R/config.R investigate smaller candidates and nearby larger values. The explicit judgment inputs are in results/decisions.csv; these are evidence decisions, not simulation outputs or automatic p-value cutoffs.

title: Methodology
text:
For a candidate sample size n, one repetition generates n observations and computes one sample mean. Repeating this B = 10,000 times produces the simulated sampling distribution of the sample mean.
The project uses a coarse-to-fine search. The initial grid is deliberately broad; earlier exploratory centers are retained for reproducibility. Targeted population-specific grids in R/config.R investigate smaller candidates and nearby larger values. title: Methodology
text:
2 Evidence used together
Each candidate sample size is assessed with a histogram, a theoretical normal overlay when appropriate, a normal Q-Q plot, skewness, excess kurtosis, empirical mean, empirical SE, theoretical mean and SE where valid, and qq_rmse.
The Standard Normal population is simulated repeatedly as a calibration benchmark. Its diagnostic ranges show how much skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE can fluctuate at B = 10,000 even when the sampling distribution is exactly normal. This benchmark contextualizes, rather than mechanically decides, the other cases.

title: Methodology
text:
3 Assumptions and exceptions
The ordinary iid finite-variance CLT does not apply unchanged to every case. Cauchy has no population mean or variance. The dependent failure process requires covariance terms in the variance of a mean. The basketball process is independent but non-identically distributed and uses the variance formula sum(p_i * (1 - p_i)) / n^2, not an iid shortcut.
The age-at-death population is synthetic and uses the instructor-provided discrete mixture exactly; it is not historical mortality data.

title: Methodology
text:
4 Decision rule
The goal is the smallest tested n I can defend, not the largest or nicest-looking plot. I assess the histogram, systematic Q-Q curvature, skewness, kurtosis, mean and SE agreement where valid, and nearby larger values together. Small discrete steps or residual tail bends may be acceptable for a practical approximation, but not for precise extreme-tail calculations. The Normal benchmark shows simulation noise; matching that noise is not a requirement.
There is no sharp biological or mathematical transition in these finite-variance cases. Adjacent candidates can be essentially indistinguishable. Where I cannot convincingly reject a smaller candidate, I report a borderline range rather than manufacture a failure reason. A selected value is a judgment under a stated tolerance, not proof that every smaller integer fails.

title: Methodology
text:
5 Sensitivity to the random seed
The primary run uses the confirmed student seed 7616. The pipeline repeats the same simulation design with seed 7617 and stores those rows in results/sensitivity_diagnostics.csv. Exact skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE values move because they are Monte Carlo estimates, but the broad conclusions are not seed-shopped: the exact Normal case remains exact in theory, Cauchy remains highly unstable through n = 5,000, and the slower finite-variance cases remain slower than the die and age mixture.
The final selections are recorded in results/final_summary.csv by scripts/finalize_summary.R. That script checks that every finite selected value is an actual tested row before copying its generated diagnostics into the summary.

title: Dependent Machine Failure
text:
First rate is 1; later rates are exp(1.25*(previous time - 1)). Each next time is conditionally Exponential. Var(Xbar) includes covariance terms, so an iid SE is inappropriate.
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{1}{n^2}\left[\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\right].
\]
Times are nonnegative, so rates are at least exp(-1.25) and conditional second moments are bounded by 2*exp(2.5). Individual finite variance is not enough to prove a dependent CLT. The supplied process starts at rate 1, without a hidden burn-in; its time-specific marginal distributions need not be identical. Compensating dependence may reduce variance relative to an iid shortcut, rather than always increasing it.

3 Evidence for my decision

3.1 Important code, in plain language
The age probabilities normalize the sum of the two instructor components. sample(age, n, replace=TRUE, prob=probability) generates independent draws. Weighted sums calculate the exact population mean and variance.
The shared simulator repeats mean(generator(n)) B times and stores one number per sample. Diagnostics are calculated from that vector, not from the original observations. Both seeds save to different directories, and loading a plotted vector checks its mean, SD and Q-Q RMSE against the matching CSV row.
I generate B = 10,000 separate samples at each n using seed 7616. Seed 7617 checks sensitivity. The full tested grid is in the CSV; this table focuses on candidates for our practical-normality review.

section: 2. Implement a reusable Q-Q RMSE function
text:
2. Implement a reusable Q-Q RMSE function
I asked (excerpt from my original implementation request):

Implement a reusable Q-Q RMSE metric.

AI said (response summary): Use one R function to standardize the simulated sample means by their empirical mean and SD, sort them, compare them with standard-Normal rank quantiles, and calculate the root-mean-square difference. Use the metric alongside plots and other diagnostics, not as proof of Normality.
What changed: AI implemented qq_rmse() in R/diagnostics.R. It uses sort((x - mean(x)) / sd(x)), qnorm(ppoints(length(x))), and the square root of the mean squared differences. The shared diagnostic function and reports reuse it instead of duplicating the calculation.
How it was checked: The existing saved-vector checks recompute Q-Q RMSE from each plotted vector and require agreement with its matching CSV row. Both seeds passed those checks in the recorded validation. I requested the feature; AI wrote and checked the implementation.

3. Implement a Normal calibration benchmark
I asked (excerpt from my original implementation request):

Use the Standard Normal population as a calibration benchmark for what simulation noise looks like even when the sampling distribution is truly normal.

AI said (response summary): Repeat genuinely Normal Monte Carlo experiments to see how skewness, excess kurtosis and Q-Q RMSE fluctuate even when Normality is exact. Save empirical diagnostic ranges for comparison, without turning them into mathematically exact acceptance thresholds.
What changed: AI implemented normal_benchmark() and summarize_normal_benchmark(). The configured design uses 30 experiments at each coarse n, with B = 10,000 sample means per experiment. It saves replicate diagnostics and their empirical 2.5th–97.5th percentile ranges.
How it was checked: The recorded final validation recomputed the calibration summary from the saved replicate diagnostics and matched it against the summary CSV. The reports explain that these ranges provide context; accepted practical approximations need not match Normal-only simulation noise. I requested the benchmark, rather than choosing an arbitrary diagnostic cutoff.

section: 4. Clarify why correct mean and SE are not enough
text:
4. Clarify why correct mean and SE are not enough
I asked (excerpt from my clarification during review):

maybe Because the mean and standard error depend on different aspects of the distribution than its overall shape?

AI said (response summary): Yes: the mean describes the center, and SE describes the spread of the sample means. Different shapes can have the same center and spread. Agreement with those theoretical quantities checks the simulation, but does not remove skewness, tail curvature or discrete Q-Q steps.
What changed: The interpretation separates center/spread validation from shape assessment. The decision argument combines mean/SE checks with histograms, Q-Q plots, skewness, excess kurtosis and nearby-n stability, rather than accepting a case solely because its SE is correct.
How it was checked: The saved Exponential evidence illustrates the distinction: at n=90, empirical and theoretical SE are close, while residual right skew and Q-Q tail bending remain. The reports present both forms of evidence. My message was a tentative clarification, not a claim that I independently verified the entire analysis.
